desc:
A university has n courses numbered 0 to n - 1. Each entry relations[i] = [prev, next] means course prev must be finished in an earlier semester than course next. The dependencies contain no cycle.

In every semester you may take at most k courses, and only courses whose prerequisites were all completed in earlier semesters. Return the minimum number of semesters needed to finish all courses.

n = 4, relations = [[1,0],[2,0],[3,0]], k = 2 -> 3
n = 5, relations = [[1,0],[2,0]],       k = 2 -> 3
n = 6, relations = [[0,1],[1,2]],       k = 3 -> 3
n = 4, relations = [],                  k = 3 -> 2

In the first example, courses 1, 2 and 3 are all prerequisites of course 0: two of them go in semester 1, the last one in semester 2, and course 0 in semester 3.
constraints: 0 ≤ prev, next < n and prev ≠ next; the graph is acyclic; pairs may repeat
hints: Without the limit k the answer is the length of the longest prerequisite chain. With the limit, a greedy 'take the first k available courses' can go wrong, because some courses unlock much more than others.
The state of the plan after each semester is just the set of finished courses. With n ≤ 12 there are only 4,096 such sets, so use dynamic programming over subsets.

dp[mask] = fewest semesters to finish exactly the courses in mask. From mask compute avail, the courses outside mask whose prerequisites all lie in mask. If avail has at most k courses take them all; otherwise try every submask of avail with exactly k courses. Transition to mask | chosen with cost +1.
editorial: After each semester, all that matters is which courses are finished. So define dp[mask] as the minimum number of semesters needed to have finished exactly the courses of mask (infinite if impossible). Store pre[v], the bitmask of the direct prerequisites of v. Course v can be taken from state mask when it is not in mask and pre[v] & ~mask == 0; let avail be the set of such courses.

From mask we choose a subset of avail of size at most k to take this semester. Finishing more courses never hurts (a larger finished set allows everything a smaller set allows), so it is enough to consider taking all of avail when it has at most k courses and exactly k courses otherwise. Iterate masks in increasing order, enumerate submasks of avail with sub = (sub - 1) & avail and use a precomputed popcount table to keep those of size k.

The answer is dp[(1 << n) - 1]. Enumerating every submask of the available set over all masks costs at most 3n steps (each course is in the mask, in the available set or in neither), which is about 531,000 for n = 12. Greedy strategies such as 'take the courses with the longest remaining chain first' are tempting but fail on some inputs, which is why the exhaustive DP is used here.
